name: Unknown (F)
text: Thank you, Micah. And good evening, Mayor and City Council. I'm Alexis Captanian, Housing Manager for the City of San Rafael, and tonight I am presenting an urgency ordinance for your consideration. The proposed ordinance would provide temporary relocation assistance and a right of return for tenants in the Canal Opportunity Zone who are displaced from their unit due to substantial rehabilitation for health and safety. So a little bit of background. In 2017, the tax cuts and Jobs Acts created tax incentives for investment in federally designated economically distressed census tracts called Opportunity Zones. To qualify for the program, a property that is acquired in the Opportunity Zone must be substantially improved over a 30 month period, a requirement that increases the risk of displacement for residential tenants due to no fault evictions. San Rafael currently has one Opportunity Zone comprised of two census tracts in the Canal neighborhood. The Opportunity Zone is shown in green light green on this map. There are approximately 1800 units in the opportunity zone and about 1500 are apartment units, giving the Opportunity Zone a much higher proportion of renters compared to the rest of the city. The Opportunity Zone has much higher rates of severe housing cost burden and overcrowding compared to the rest of San Rafael and Marin County. In March 2021, the City Council adopted an ordinance requiring property owners to pay relocation assistance to tenants evicted in the Opportunity Zone for substantial rehabilitation. Since October 2022, city staff has reviewed permanent relocation payments for 31 tenant households who were evicted on the grounds of substantial rehabilitation for health and safety within the Canal Opportunity Zone. Additionally, the city processed permit applications for another 37 units in the Opportunity Zone where the property owner indicated that a no fault eviction did not occur. By comparison, in the year and a half prior to that, the city did not review any relocation payments in the Opportunity Zone. Due to the tight rental market in San Rafael and Marin county, it is extremely difficult for displaced tenants tenants to secure other housing. Staff has received reports of displaced Opportunity Zone tenants moving out of Marin, doubling up with other families or becoming unhoused and moving into their cars. San Rafael's 2023 through 2031 housing element and the City Council's goals and objectives direct staff to conduct stakeholder engagement and evaluate citywide tenant protection policies. And staff is working on data collection and planning community engagement for this effort. The proposed Urgency Ordinance, which is specific to the Canal Opportunity Zone, is an interim measure to prevent further displacement of families due to substantial rehabilitation while the city undergoes this broader process regarding citywide tenant protection policies so the proposed ordinance temporarily amends an existing San Rafael policy called Cause Required for Eviction, which regulates the grounds for eviction in properties with three or more dwelling units. Under the current policy, a property owner can evict a tenant to perform substantial repairs. If this happens, the property owner is required to pay the tenant a relocation assistance payment, but the tenant does not have a right to return to the unit when the repairs are completed. The proposed Urgency ordinance amends the existing policy for the Opportunity Zone only, removing substantial rehabilitation as a cause for eviction. In most cases, the proposed ordinance would require property owners to offer tenants the right to return to their unit after repairs are completed. If the tenant wants to return to the unit after repairs are completed, the tenant must continue to pay rent while the unit is being repaired. In order to maintain the existing lease while the unit is being repaired, the landlord must either pay the tenant a daily amount to cover the cost of temporary lodging or the landlord has the option to provide a comparable unit on the property or another property in San Rafael. If the tenant does not want to be temporarily relocated and returned to the unit following repairs, the tenant can choose to move out permanently and is eligible for a Permanent Relocation Assistance payment, which already exists under city policy. This policy would be in effect through December 31, 2026, in line with the expiration of the Opportunity Zone tax benefits. The package under consideration tonight also includes a resolution specifying payment amounts. The daily temporary relocation payments proposed are $250 per day during the first 29 days of displacement based on the cost of hotel, motel and short term rental options in Marin county and then starting on day 30, the payment would be based on either the tenant's monthly lease rent or the current fair market rent, whichever is greater. So, for example, the 2024 fair market rent for a two bedroom is $3,359, so the daily payment would be about $112. The proposed ordinance requires staff review of relocation plans during the permitting process, and so the resolution proposes an administrative fee based on the fully burdened rate of the staff. Reviewer so to recap, the Urgency Ordinance would amend municipal code chapter 10.105, which is the cause required for eviction policy. It would also amend municipal code chapter 10.111, which is the Relocation Assistance and Opportunity zones The Permanent Relocation Assistance Assistance. And then the resolution would establish temporary relocation assistance, payment amounts and an administrative processing fee. And this policy would be in effect through December 31, 2026, in the Canal Opportunity Zone. The City Council has the following options to consider. Adopt the urgency ordinance and resolution. Adopt the urgency ordinance and resolution with modifications. Direct staff to return with more information or take no action. I'm joined by Director Micah Hinkle, and we are available to take your questions.

text: Good evening, mayor, council members. Thank you for having me here tonight to talk about the amended ordinance. Before we get into the details of the ordinance, I just want to give you a summary of the current state of the law and how we got here tonight where we're going to be proposing some amendments to our current or existing camping regulations. So as, as you know, in 2019, there was a seminar criminal case in the Ninth Circuit called Martin v. Boise. And in that case, the ninth Circuit determined that criminal enforcement of sleeping on public property by an individual who does not have alternative shelter available to them constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under the eighth amendment of the US Constitution. But I do want to point out that while that, that underlying determination was made by the court, the court was also very clear that cities still have a lot of latitude to regulate around the edges, and that includes regulating the time, place and manner by which individuals would be permitted to, to camp or sleep on public property. Since that time, which is now five years ago, five years, there's been a host, as you can imagine, of dozens of cases that have come down considering Martin v. Boise and then other details around activities or behaviors related to sleeping or camping on, on public property. This is just kind of a list, a sample of them. There's cases considering how to determine whether an individual is involuntarily homeless and whether that the, the determination there is whether you have the number of homeless persons exceeds the number of shelter beds in a certain jurisdiction or whether that analysis should be based more on the particularized individual circumstances. Also the quality type of alternative shelter, whether personal property can be seized, and the procedures around that. As I mentioned, the time, place and manner restrictions. And then also whether a city has left open sufficient public property in a jurisdiction for the number of homeless individuals there in order to sleep. So this area of law isn't in a lot of flux considering the number of cases that are currently being litigated. And I did want to point out, and it's mentioned in our staff report tonight, that there is a, a case up at the Supreme Court now. It's going to be actually heard on oral argument next week, and that's the city of Grants Pass versus Johnson. And in that case, they will be considering the Martin v. Boise determination by the Ninth Circuit. So we'll be watching that case and then looking at the city's camping regulations in light of existing law. So almost a year ago now, in July 2023, you adopted a new regulation for camping on public property. And the, this was a time, place and manner restriction for individuals sleeping in San Rafael on public property. And it was a, a, a novel approach. There's cities that have adopted kind of similar types of ordinances, but in our case, case, our ordinance, which is our existing ordinance that's on the books today, the rule is that campsites cannot occupy more than 100 square foot for one person. Or if there's multiple people that want to sleep together or camp together, they can occupy a space no greater than 200 square foot. And then there's also a distancing rule whereby campsites must be separated by 200ft apart from each other. And then there's some other kind of What I would call like, buffer zones that are written into the ordinances or areas where camping is strictly prohibited. And one of the rules in there includes that individuals cannot camp within 100ft of playgrounds. The ordinance was to take effect last August, but prior to the date of the ordinance taking effect, the city was sued. That lawsuit, which is Boyd versus City of San Rafael, is currently ongoing in the Northern District in the federal court. So we do not have a resolution on that case at this time. So back in October in the Boyd case, Judge Edward Chen of the Northern District Cal Northern District Court issued a preliminary injunction order. Preliminary injunction order will be in effect through the pendency of the litigation or until a further order of the court. So it is temporary, but it does apply to our current situation. And in that preliminary injunction order, the judge did permit the city to enforce our ordinance, but under modified spacing and distancing rules. And those include that we would permit up to campsites of a size of 400 square feet. So our current ordinance allows 200 square feet. So it would allow a double the size of a campsite and up to four persons, which would equal 100 square foot per person within a. Within a campsite. And then instead of being separated by 200ft, he essentially cut that distance in half to 100ft. But also what was very significant about the order is that he also required the city to develop and execute on an allocation and registration process by which individuals would. That the city would track where individuals were camping within the city so that they would know that they were not running afoul of the law if they were to camp at a certain spot in the city. We since October, our staff, including Chris and Mel and his team, have worked tirelessly to execute on the preliminary injunction order procedures. And we found that the implementation is exceedingly difficult and challenging. And we've made very little progress to actually see any beneficial effect effects of the ordinance. There's numerous reasons for that. I will mention one of the main barriers has been the number of requests that we've received under the Americans with Disabilities act by individuals who are requesting more space than the 100 square foot that they're allotted. And each of those take an individualized assessment. So those have taken a lot of staff time as well. So we're continuing to litigate this case, and we've been trying to resolve it. And that includes numerous meetings between city staff and representatives of the homeless community. So what we are proposing tonight is a pivot from where we were back in July and where we are Today. And what we are proposing is an amended ordinance ordinance which keeps some spacing and distancing rules, but aligns the rules to Judge Chen's order and also some other adjustments to the ordinance. So I'll talk about those details. So the ordinance is written substantively in three major parts. The first section lists public properties that are strictly prohibited to camping. Those sites are listed on this slide. So examples are open spaces and city parking garages. These sites for the most part, have been prohibited to camping for years now. For example, open spaces, which are the kind of wildfire areas, areas you know, in the hills in San Francisco, are prohibited decamping because of the significant fire wildfire risk. text: Thank you and good evening Mayor Kate and city council members. My name is Scott Eberle. I'm currently a lieutenant, San Police Department. Out of those categories, Sanfel Police Department only has equipment in seven of the listed categories. To continue using military equipment, the law requires that each year the City Council review the annual report and renew the ordinance it has adopted approving the funding acquisition and use of military equipment. In May of 2022, the City Council adopted Ordinance 2007, adding Chapter 2.52 to the San Rafael Municipal Code to establish the requirements for approval and annual review of our military equipment policy. The San Rafael Police Department Military Equipment Annual Report for calendar year 2023 was attached to the staff report and it included the six required pieces of information. It outlined how the equipment was used and the purpose of its use, any complaints concerning the military equipment, results of any internal audits, costs associated with the equipment and use, full inventory of the equipment we possess, and if we intend to acquire any additional equipment next year. This was outlined in detail in the annual report, but in summary it included the use of The Marin County Sheriff's Office Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Category 1 six times, otherwise known as a drone, the armored rescue vehicle in category 2 three times, and the less than lethal impact device category 14, once also noted in the report. The San Rafael Police Department did not receive any complaints about using military equipment during the reporting period, nor did any internal audits reveal any policy violations. At the July 17th city council meeting of last year, the Council approved the replacement of 10 aging end of service patrol rifles. I want to report that those 10 rifles were taken to a disposal site where the weapons were melted down and destroyed. Besides the above inventory actions, the inventory of the military equipment has not changed in 2023 and it's attached to the annual report. There are no new proposed items for the military equipment list in 2024, except for that we are asking for the replacement of 10 patrol rifles that are at the end of their service life, just as we did last year. The equipment that falls under the definition of military equipment that the San Rafael Police Department has and is used to de escalate violent situations. I want to underscore that the pieces of equipment are used to create time, distance and provide cover to facilitate the time needed to deal with these high risk situations in Every situation, whether violent or not, every officer factors in three things upon initial contact. That's time, distance and cover. Having more time to make decisions gives us more time to weigh options and formulate and discuss contingencies and strategies which create a better opportunity for success and peaceful resolution. The distance to or from any problem will change the tactics and strategy. For example, if a violent subject is within a couple feet of an officer is much different and way more imminent than an officer can stand back 30 to 50 yards and deal with that situation. It'll give the officer more time to react, plan and de escalate. Cover Cover is a term that is used to describe being in a safe area behind ballistic protection. Cover can come from many forms such as an engine block of a vehicle, a large tree or an armored vehicle. All of these pieces of equipment that are outlined in our military equipment inventory list are are necessary to create time, distance and cover. Without these pieces of equipment, the possibility for peaceful outcomes is diminished and the chances for injuries are greatly increased. I do want to underscore again that the San Rafael Police Department prioritizes preventative strategies over reactionary tactics. Some of our preventative strategies that we highlight in the center for Police Department are community policing, crime prevention through environmental design, youth programs, neighborhood watch programs, community outreach and education, partnerships with other agencies, the use of technology such as ALPRs, proactive policing and specialized units, just to name a few. I really wish there would never be a need to deploy any of the equipment that I listed on the Military Equipment Annual Report. But it is better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it. In conclusion, these pieces of equipment are used to contain the actions of violent endangered subjects and influence their intentions that help us move toward a goal of a peaceful resolution. The equipment that we use and have are available to us is critical for a peaceful resolution for those individuals involved, our officers and the community as a whole. The city's been in litigation over a camping ordinance that the City Council passed last summer in August of 2023. This ordinance aimed to create a regulatory framework to help mitigate for the health and safety issues that are created by homeless encampments. An enormous amount of staff, time and energy has been spent and along with our our service providers over the last nine months responding to the court's rulings and orders and establishing a new camping ordinance that we can utilize enforcement tool when necessary, which was passed just this past March. That new camping ordinance does set maximum campsite sizes to 200 square feet for individuals and 400 square feet for more than one individual, and establishes buffer zones from schools. For example, you can't camp within 250ft of a school, within 10ft of a private property line, and 10ft from utility infrastructure. So that new ordinance is something we can implement. However, we are still in active litigation over the prior camping ordinance. This litigation that was filed against the city by the California Homeless Union follows the 2018 Supreme Court decision called Martin vs. Boise, in which the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that cities cannot criminalize a person for sleeping on public property and that the city cannot ban camping on public properties unless there are adequate shelter space available for that individual to stay, which unfortunately, we do not have enough adequate shelter here in Marin County. Recently, the Supreme Court heard arguments about a month ago regarding the related 9th Circuit ruling in Johnson vs. Grant's Pass. However, the city was blocked by the federal court last Friday who ruled that while the individuals living in the structures are to relocate to tents along the Mahone Creek path tomorrow, their structures must remain in place pending the outcome of their peer appeals on encroachment right of way violations, which are scheduled to be considered at an administrative hearing on June 25th. text: Good evening, Honorable Mayor Kate and Members of City Council. John Stefanski Assistant City Manager I'm here tonight with Mel Burnett, our housing and homelessness analyst and really excited to be here because this is a opportunity for us as staff to come and present a comprehensive update on the city's approach to homelessness. So tonight's presentation, we have a number of things that we're going to cover and we'll be providing a brief background and some context setting, as well as an overview of the city's approach and response to homelessness to date. For the council tonight, there are two recommended actions. The first is consideration of amendments to the city's camping ordinance. And then the second is consideration of contracts the city will need to enter into for the development and operation of the planned sanctioned camping area and for providing homelessness related services more generally in the city. So by way of background, as of the most recent point in time count In Marin County 2024, there are 1,090 individuals experiencing homelessness in the county. Of these individuals, 788 were unsheltered at the time of the count and 217 were chronically homeless. Now, I'll add that this represents a 2.77% decrease from the 2022 point in time count, but for San Rafael, the 2024 numbers are not yet available. So based off of the 2022 count, we estimate around 348 individuals experiencing homelessness in the city. But to supplement this work, the city did a survey last year of individuals who were living along the Mahone Creek path and of the people who were living there had done so for over a year and that two thirds of those people had lived in San Rafael for over a decade. Now, the county has had a lot of great success in recent years and housing individuals experiencing homelessness. Since 2017, they have been able to house 737 chronically homeless individuals and 94% of those folks remain housed to this day. Day, however, as we saw on the previous slide, I think particularly relevant for the discussion this evening is that there's still much more work to be done as we only have 291 shelter beds available in the county for over a thousand individuals. So turning our attention to San Rafael, we're going to spend some time on this slide. Not a year, but we'll be here for a little bit. The city has been effectively blocked from enforcing our camping on public property regulations since August of last year. So we've been at this now for over a year, really. And as you'll recall, it was this council who in 2023 had made amendments to the city's camping ordinance to comply with the then governing Martin v. Boise decision, and three days before that ordinance was to take effect act, the city was sued in federal court based off of the Americans with Disability act as well as claims that there was a state created danger. The court entered a temporary restraining order and then later a preliminary injunction that effectively blocked the city's ability to enforce these camping regulations from December to February of last year. And then this year, the city attempted in good faith to implement the direction of the court, which at the time it sought to have the city work with the California Homeless Union and individuals and members along the Mahone Creek Path area encampment to designate set campsites for individuals and establish voluntary compliance with the direction of the court. However, this work was ultimately abandoned because we were not able to achieve the level of cooperation that was needed in order for that approach to be effective. So shortly thereafter, the city refocused its attention towards amending the camping ordinance to address the concerns of the court and to create a regulatory framework that could we that we could ultimately use to mitigate the impacts of encampments. And the City council passed this updated ordinance in April of this year. Following this, the city filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, and earlier this month the court granted this motion allowing the city to proceed with implementing the amended camping ordinance. And I'll have more to share on that implementation here shortly. However, I will note that during the time of the preliminary injunction, the city worked to identify other regulatory avenues to address the public health and safety concerns related to encampments in the city. As you may recall, in October and November of last year we enforced the fire code to abate fire risks associated with the proliferation of wooden structures and wooden pallets and encampments in the city. And then in December of last year, the city manager issued an order prohibited camping on Lindaro Street. And so, as you'll see on the slide here, we have a before picture of Lindaro street and then a picture of Lindaro street shortly after that order went into effect. And you do have the staff report of a little presentation, hopefully get us through the bulk of it. I would note that in the agenda item after just the staff report is the resolution that we're asking the council to consider this evening and as an exhibit to the resolution is effectively the clean copy of what the updated fee schedule would look like. Assuming council is comfortable with the staff recommendation, as is the practice. We've also included in the agenda packet a redline version so that council and public can see all the changes. Most of it is cleaning up. I just, I'll highlight that. We'll, we'll touch on the substantive changes and then the very last attachment is specific to the recreation program fees that are laid out separately at the end of the agenda item. So again, by way brief background, our master fee schedule is essentially the means by which the city council approves and adopts fees for charges for services to recover costs associated with delivering those services either at full cost recovery or at subsidized level. I Note that the 2425 budget has about $22 million in revenue from charges for services. So it is a significant component to the budget. The current fee Schedule and the recommendations that are for you bit this evening are consistent with the requirements in state law and state constitution around what we can and cannot charge and recover fees for. And while there are a lot of areas where current council policy is established to recover full costs, there's also a lot of programs and services that for which we by policy do not recover the full costs. And those typically are the ones with significant public benefit. So there's a whole range of cost recovery in the fee schedule. Council may recall that the last comprehensive update actually took place in December of 2022, just coming out perhaps of the pandemic in the council action at that time, I think it had been almost five, six, seven years before there had really been a comprehensive update. So what we're trying to do is kind of maintain updates on an annual basis so that we don't fall all foreign arrears and then have to do massive updates. So the council approved the fee schedule in December of 22 establishing target cost recovery levels. Significantly, the council also authorized at that time an automatic annual increases based on consumer price index, AKA inflationary adjustments, and also laid out the implementation schedule for that that. Part of the reason why we're here this evening is that pursuant to that action, the CPI index that would apply to fees as of the start of this fiscal year July 1st is 2.37%. And so there's a whole host of fees in the schedule that are simply going up by the CPI adjustment. I want to give you an example in the current fee schedule, this is also a link to the website. It's organized in these 14 separate categories. So each one has its own. And we also modeled this report and the attachments to follow along with this. But it's. And then an example of a page from the fee scheduler section that shows the fee. It shows also the cost recovery targets that have been established by the council. And so these are presented on the website again in these 14 sections or chapters. So for the 2425 update, again, there's a number of revisions that are being made that admittedly do not require council approval. That's where we're not proposing to modify the fee, where the fees are simply going up by the council approved CPI adjustment. And there's also again some cleanup work going through and eliminating fees in the fee schedule for services that the city is no longer providing or we've changed how that service is being provided. The areas that we're going to focus on briefly this evening that do require formal council action is a handful of areas where staff is proposing fee increases that will exceed the CPI index, particularly to either maintain target cost recovery levels, the costs have been exceeding the CPI as well as a couple of categories of new fees that are proposed to be added to the fee schedule. I also note on this slide that the council will recall that on the heels of approving the 2425 budget, the council already took action related to fees associated with the city's child care program and that took place on July 15th and those were enacted early, if you will, to coincide with the academic year for which those fees are set. Given that list that I shared earlier, there's actually no fee adjustments proposed in few of our categories here. Library, admin citations, sewer drainage and then only CPI based fees in some of the fee schedules related to several of the permits that are handled through our planning and building department. I am going to highlight now the areas where we are proposing some changes and in some increases that do require council action. If it works, I'm going to go through these. We also have staff from the various departments that can hopefully assist for any questions that the council or the public may have on this. The two things I'll highlight on the police services and again this is in the attachment three they're proposing to modify an existing fee related to false alarm response. If you can see in the strikeout, currently there's a fee set, I believe it's $140 for, for the third or more responses. So after you get to three and after three it's $140 per response. And this is proposing to be just a kind of a graduated fee schedule. So there would be a fee charged with the first and second response less than the current fee and then $150 for the third and then adding I think $50. So basically there's an incentive to not wait till you have the third or fourth, fourth false alarm response before being cited. And then the other one that we're calling out here and this is to basically be consistent with changes in state law where there's, there's now an increase in the maximum amount that can be collected under dui, collision restitutions, driving under the influence. And so that's, this is an increase that's consistent with, with new state law. Another area in the police services. This is just an example of some of the cleanup we're removing from the fee schedule fees that are no longer assessed, some of which are for instance the massage establishments. These are now covered in our building and safety section of the fee schedule through the planning department no longer under the police. Also based on change in state law, I believe, since the pandemic, we're no longer authorized, if you will, to issue permits for several categories of street vendors. And the last one, I think is the taxi permits, which is now run through the county in terms of the permitting. So the police department's no longer in the business. So this again just an example of a cleanup in that category. One of the significant recommendations of FOIA this evening is related to fire services fee and specifically the charges for ambulance transport. And here you have the advanced life support kind of bundle base rate and then the component rates. Just speaking briefly about this, there's two factors that are driving this recommendation, and it's largely based on both the cost of providing the service, but also an analysis of other jurisdictions that provide transport. And the recommendation is to essentially increase the fees to go from a 55% cost recovery level to roughly 75% cost recovery level, which is essentially what the neighboring jurisdictions are charging. We did cover this again, briefly, as was mentioned earlier in the finance subcommittee. And I'll just say the fire staff is here to assist. But these fees are by and large paid by the insurers of the patients that avail themselves of the transport. When you have individuals that may not have adequate insurance or lack insurance, these are not charged to the patient. So it's really a mechanism to maximize the cost recovery of our services from the insurance providers that paid the bill. In the planning area, there's again some cleanup. But one change that we are calling out is essentially codifying in the master fee schedule a series of fees related to the streamlined housing development applications. This was an ordinance that I believe the council adopt last April. The city's actually been charging this fees, you know, based on equivalent fees that are already on the books relative to the same level of effort and time that's taken. But this essentially adds the fee and codifies it in the master fee schedule. So these fees have been charged, but we're now reflecting them as discrete separate fees within the fee schedule. Main one I'll point out, for public works fees, they're adding to the fee schedule, a category for work associated with special events set up. Traffic control has always been a little bit of a challenge between all the various departments. The proposal is to essentially charge actual cost associated with this for most special events. And so we're also calling out that we are looking at how this fee would then be applied, potentially with some discounts or fee waivers for city sponsored events. So there's a Distinction between folks that seek to um, close streets for these events and some of the events that the city, um, has an interest in continuing to sponsor. So this at least sets the. The basis for it at at full cost recovery. The last section of the um proposals really have to do with the recreation fees. And so again, these are in attachment four of your staff report. Recreation staff is constantly looking at their fees and their fee structures, looking to sort of hit that sweet spot between maximizing cost recovery but still making the programs accessible to all the residents and comparing our rates to other or agencies in the area. In general, the recommendation is to increase the recreation fees by 5% with a couple of exceptions that are listed here. The fall Kerr Cultural center and aquatic fees are recommended to have a slightly higher increase. And they've really identified areas where again, the CPI level adjustment does not keep up with our costs in relation to maintaining targets. And I think the next slide really summarizes. There's a number of fees that are, you know, kind of where there's a deposit that is placed. There's no change in the deposit fees. 5% increase for facility rentals and park and field FEES and again 15% increase for use of the fall Kirk Cultural center fees as well as for the aquatics program. Council's also aware that I believe we're two years into a pilot program for a fall and winter aquatics. And the recommendation is to kind of transition from that year to year pilot to a standard offering. And I think because the rates were somewhat subsidized in the pilot program, the full cost recovery or the appropriate cost recovery target for that program is suggested. A 22% fee increase on the fall and winter aquatics. We also do note that per council previous policy, selected programs both at Pickleweed and at the Borough Community center offered at 50% discount from the. From the maximum rates. Just wrapping up here, the recommendations before you. The CPI adjustments basically take effect automatically. But the fees that we're bringing to you this Evening outside of CPI adjustment, we're proposing to be effective January 1st, so start of the calendar year going forward, with the exception of the winterfall aquatics program fees that would essentially be effective October 1st so that they can be implemented for this upcoming period. And then lastly, I will note that most of the recommendations that are before you were contemplated as we were putting the budget together because we figured that we would need to adjust the fees. Overall there's about $23 million I said in charges for services. The bulk of the recommendations in this report generate about 3/4 of a million Dollars in additional revenue across all funds, which has already been factored into the budget. The one exception is the emergency medical services fees and the ambulance transport that the fire department's been working on. And if approved on an annualized basis, that's about a $400,000 increase, which is significant in relation to both the budget for the fire department, but also the interplay between our general fund support and the paramedic tax. So this fee, I think, admittedly will reduce the pressure going forward in terms of the need to address the level of increase in a future paramedic tax. So the department's really looking to maximize revenues where there's revenues to be collected. So again, the recommendation before you is to adopt the resolution authorizing the update in the master fee schedule. And exhibit A to that resolution provides the clean copy of what would be the fees if approved as recommended. With that, we're open. Any questions?
